Hi Fabiana, it's Daniel from Sales. I heard you're presenting at the QBR on Monday, so here's a heads-up. Last quarter, the CFO threw a curveball at every presenter. He asked the logistics team why freight costs had gone up, and their manager lost his train of thought halfway through the answer. It was painful to watch. My advice is simple: get to the point in the first sentence, give one number, and stop. If he asks something you can't answer, don't guess. Say you'll circle back by the end of the week, and then actually do it. He respects that. Oh, and one more thing: he hates slides with more than three bullet points. Good luck, and call me if you want to rehearse on Sunday.

Hello Fabiana, this is Priya Nair. Thank you for agreeing to present the supplier update on Monday. Let me explain the format, because it's a little unusual. Each presenter has five minutes, and then the leadership team asks questions for ten. We call it the rapid round. The questions are meant to show how well you think on your feet, not to catch you out. I'd recommend that you open with the decision you need from us, not with the history. The board already knows about the fire in Penang. What they don't know yet is what you want them to approve. A short hesitation before an answer is fine; it shows you're thinking. What we want to avoid is a long, rambling answer that never lands. If you need a moment, rephrase the question. See you on Monday at nine.

Fabiana plans her opening for the rapid round. First, she opens with the decision: the board is asked to approve the dual-supplier contract for 2027. Second, she gives the backstory in one sentence: Penang had been running at full capacity for months when the fire hit. Third, she reports the latest news with care: it is thought that the new line will be ready by November. Then she makes her case with a question: wouldn't one supplier leave us exposed again? Finally, she closes with a plan: should the port close again, the team will reroute through Singapore within forty-eight hours.
